utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber will be sitting this afternoon in the absence of Judge Chowhan, who is absent for urgent personal reasons. The other Judges of the Chamber have decided that it's in the interests of justice to do so. The same will be the situation tomorrow. Tomorrow also we will be without Judge Nosworthy, who will quite independently be absent on the ground of urgent personal reasons. Your next witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is General Klaus Naumann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Naumann.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. We've received a number of documents, including the transcript of your evidence in the previous trial of Slobodan Milosevic. So the Trial Chamber is already fairly well-informed about your evidence; however, you will be examined as a witness who's here as what the Prosecution describe as a live witness. I can't honestly say we've had any dead ones, but we'll in due course be looking at these documents. The extent to which we explore them in court will depend on the way in which the questions are asked but, first of all, to examine you will be on behalf of the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I begin the questions I just want to indicate this witness is being presented as a combination 92 ter and live witness. He does speak to the paragraphs of the indictment noted in the witness notification. For purposes of Rule 92 ter, Your Honour, we're proposing both his testimony in Milosevic on the 13th and 14th of June, 2002, and the notes and summary of his interview and proofing in June of 1999 and March 2002. And to begin, I would like to hand the witness a hard copy of his trial testimony in Milosevic. For the record, this is Exhibit P2512.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have a chance to review your trial testimony from the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I had a chance to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of doing that, did you note some corrections that you wanted to make in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, there are some typos in it, which we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I can hand the witness a hard copy of P2561 which is the supplemental information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I would ask if you could take a look at that and tell us if you recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that contain the changes that you noted with regard to the transcript as well as some additional information you wanted to provide to us regarding your evidence in that transcript?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: These are the changes, and the document reflects properly the additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, with regard then to your transcript, having made those corrections, are you satisfied and can you attest now to the Court that the transcript as so corrected accurately reflects your evidence and the answers you would give now if asked about the same matters under oath?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have one more document I'd like to show you. This is a hard copy of Exhibit P1767. These are the notes of an interview and proofing notes of you from the 17th of June, 1999, and the 25th and 26th of March, 2002, with OTP representatives. Before today, did you have a chance to look over that document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I had a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is -- can you tell us whose signature that is on the bottom right-hand side of each page?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's still mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And having reviewed those notes, are you satisfied that they are a true and accurate representation of your testimony or the evidence you would give in this case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: This is an accurate reflection of what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you would give the same answers today if you were asked the same questions regarding those matters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note in paragraph 36, there is a reference to an attached list of significant Serb and VJ activity. And, General, I should indicate to you that we at the OTP do not currently have a copy of that. I'm aware that that was provided by you at the time, but we've been unable to locate our copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're continuing the search, contacting former investigators and Prosecutors, but we do not have that document at the moment. I see Mr. Cepic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, it is for these reasons mentioned by my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, it is my humble opinion that this paragraph, paragraph 36, should be redacted, taken out of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that submission based on the absence of the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm worried by this document, not because I would be concerned about whether Mr. Naumann's thoughts and words are included, but this is what worries me. First of all, it bears the sign of confidentiality; therefore, it should bear a stamp. Second of all, we don't see who drafted the document. There are no signatures there, apart from Mr. Naumann's. The third reason I wanted to state was that since obviously it was not drafted by Mr. Naumann and it wasn't given under oath, it represents an interview, a conversation, between Mr. Naumann and someone else. We see all the paragraphs having headings, subheadings, and conclusions. And if this is to be tendered, I will agree only to the part which refers directly to Mr. Naumann's words and thoughts and whether we -- this is indeed confidential or not and we also need to know who drafted it. There are headings everywhere, all over the place, the role of NATO, for example, paragraphs 29, 35, 40, and everything else that has been said up until now. I am a bit worried about the form of this document. It is rather unusual. I'm not insisting on anything. And I believe Mr. Naumann when he says that he would repeat the same thing now, but in my jurisdiction this would not be an acceptable document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's safe to say, Mr. Fila, that in many jurisdictions it wouldn't be seen as an acceptable way in which to present the material. Here, however, the rules are different, and the question is whether a document ought to be before the Trial Chamber in the interests of justice. And unless you can identify something that you think would be contrary to the interests of justice by having this document, it's difficult to see that there would be a basis for excluding. Mr. Cepic has tried to identify one particular reason; and if there are any others, then you should identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood Mr. Fila to be talking about the notes of interview as a whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- whereas, Mr. Cepic is just referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I don't know who drafted it. You managed to -- were you able to establish who authored the document. It would be in proper order to inform us who else was there. Second, the headings don't come from Mr. Naumann. I find these things unacceptable whenever there is a heading as of item 1 onwards and specifically items 35 and 40, that's why I object to the entire document. I believe Mr. Naumann though when he says he would repeat the same thing now, but I have objection to the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, do you consider that these headings accurately reflect the nature of the contents of the paragraphs to which they are headings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the headings reflect properly the content of the subparagraphs in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall repel both objections and admit all three documents in their entirety. I hope, Mr. Fila, that the headings to some -- the comment about the headings to some extent reassures you. It is our intention to find out who else was present at the interview in the course of the examination; and as far as Mr. Cepic's objection is concerned, I also can confirm that I was concerned to explore this matter. And it will be explored in the course of the evidence and of course it may affect the weight of what's said, that we don't have the document available. Bearing in mind also that it was cross-examined upon in the previous trial. However, in general, each of the points made by counsel really go to weight, rather than to the admissibility of the document or any part of it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will take up one related matter then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to your notes of interview and proofing, Exhibit P1767, who, General, if you know, was involved in preparing this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: This was done by Mr. Ryneveld who was then doing the job which you had in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. Dirk Ryneveld from the Office of the Prosecution and yourself?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I would ask you to state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: My name is Klaus Naumann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand you are retired from the military. You were a professional soldier in the German army from 1958 until when?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I served in the German armed forces from October 1958 to the 31st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of work do you currently do, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I live up to the many, what I should say non-paid commitments which you have to do after your retirement. One of them, for instance, is to be a member of the supervisory board of the Konrad Adenauer Organisation in Germany, and I could list a couple more of them. And I assumed more recently the chairmanship of the supervisory board of a mid-sized German company called OWR, which is focussed on the equipment of fire brigades and armed forces in the field of NBC defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And NBC is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Nuclear, biological, and chemical defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you give the Court, briefly, a background of your career in the military. We don't have that in your notes?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I joined in 1958, changing my initial ideas to study archaeology under the impressions of the Hungarian uprise in 1956 and became a regular military officer. It began with two years education at the German armed forces war academy, I think would be the proper English translation, and the artillery school. I was in the artillery, then I served in the self-propelled artillery instruction battalion 51 in Germany in various functions, starting from a forward observer to the battalion's fire direction officer. I changed from there to Wetzlar in Hesse to command a 155 battery, self-propelled. From there I was transferred to Duelmen, which I would say is a fortified crossroad somewhere south of Muenster in Germany. And there I served as a regimental fire direction officer in the 7th artillery regiment. From there I was selected to be a student at the general staff and command college for two and a half years in Hamburg. After completion of my course, I had my first assignment in the Ministry of Defence in the long-term planning section before I was picked by the vice Chief of Defence Staff to be his personal staff officer for two years. From there I went on to serve as the G3, which is more or less the Chief of Staff of an armoured brigade in Koblenz, then I commanded a self-propelled artillery battalion, 155, in Hamburg in the northern part of Hesse. After that, I returned to the Ministry of Defence to be responsible for the personnel management of the general staff officers of the German army, then I served in Brussels as a full colonel then in the "polmil" section of the German military representative to NATO. That was from 1981 to 1983. Thereafter, I attended the course at the Royal College of Defence Studies in London. And after this one year, which I still regard as one of the most fascinating experiences in my military life, I was selected to command a mechanised infantry brigade, mechanised infantry brigade 30 garrisoned in Ellwangen in Baden-Wurttenberg. After two years in command, I had to return to the Ministry of Defence under promotion to the rank of brigadier-general and was major responsible for the long-term planning of the German armed forces. This I did until 1998, and then I was appointed to be the -- what the Americans would call a J5, the assistant Chief of Staff for military policy, operations, arms control, nuclear strategy, in the Ministry of Defence in Bonn. Thereafter, I was picked to be the commanding general of the 1st German Corps in Muenster; and following that, I became Chief of Defence Staff of Germany starting this four-star assignment in October 1991 and ending it on the 6th of February 1996. Particularly fascinating period, since in that time I saw the dissolution of the east German armed forces, re-unification of my country, and the first out-of-area deployment of the German armed forces to Somalia, Cambodia, and then to Yugoslavia -- or former Yugoslavia I should correctly say. And in February 1996, I assumed my last military assignment as chairman of the NATO military committee. The job of the chairman is described in the document P1767.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there any higher military position in NATO than the position of chairman?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you held that position from when?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I held it from 14th of February, 1996, until 6th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that normally a set period of time, that position?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It is a period of -- normally, it's a period of three years; and as I discussed earlier, I had been asked to stay a little longer for two reasons. First of all, we had in front of us the preparation of the 50th anniversary summit of NATO in Washington in April 1999 with inter alia a new strategic concept was about to be agreed by the heads of states. And then of course the ongoing crisis in Yugoslavia and in Kosovo led by superiors -- my political superiors at NATO to the conclusion that I should stay on a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how is one chosen for that position? Who picks the chairman?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, it's a -- as far as I know, it's the only four-star appointment for which you are elected; but in sharp contrast to political life, there is no campaign preceding that. Your colleagues -- well, the chiefs of the defence staff of the then-16 NATO nations look at their colleagues, discuss among themselves, and suddenly someone comes and says, How would you feel? Could you be the next chairman? In my case, I was approached by the British and the American Chief of Defence Staff in 1994. I then went back to ask my government whether they might be willing to agree to that, and this had to be a decision to be taken at the highest political level, say in Germany at the chancellor level. And when Chancellor Kohl agreed to the nomination, I had to throw my gauntlet into the bull pit and was selected I think in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those who vote are your fellow military --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: These were the chiefs of defence staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- counterpart?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: -- of the 16 nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, we know in 1998 or 1999 NATO became involved or engaged in Kosovo. How did that first come about? What brought Kosovo to NATO's attention?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, a defensive alliance such as NATO has the duty and the obligation to look at the situation in its -- I should say strategic perimeter. The former Yugoslavia was not too far away from NATO territory, and after all I think NATO's territory was affected by the tragedy in Yugoslavia since we had hundreds of thousands of refugees in our country. As I remember, for instance, in Germany we had at the peak some 400.000 refugees. And when we saw the unrest which started in early 1998, Kosovo was put on the agenda of the foreign ministers' meeting in Luxembourg in April 1998. I think that was the first time NATO really discussed the situation in Kosovo at a political level. Before that we had looked at situation briefings, but this was nothing but a reflection of what was going on based on the information which was available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you and NATO aware then in April of 1998 of the United Nations Security Council Resolution Number 1160 that had been passed on the 31st of March concerning Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Of course we followed the events of -- in the United Nations as closely as we could, and of course we took note of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And likewise, the subsequent UN Security Council Resolution in September the 23rd, 1998?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, those are P455 and 456 which are already in evidence by order of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What actions did NATO take in 1998 concerning this problem?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, at the foreign ministers' meeting, NATO did not much more than to express serious and to indicate to the outside world that a continuation of the situation in Kosovo and a further escalation could have been an impact on NATO's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your written evidence in your prior testimony, General, we know that you participated in three separate visits to Belgrade in late 1998 and early 1999 to meet with Mr. Milosevic about Kosovo. And that first trip was the 15th of October with General Clark and the NATO Secretary-General Mr. Javier Solana. First of all, General Clark, what was his position vis-a-vis your position?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: General Clark was the Supreme Allied Commander Europe. In the hierarchy of NATO, he is -- well, he is a little bit below the Chairman of The Military Committee, also there is no direct line of command. The chain of command runs from the Secretary-general to the Supreme Allied Commander Europe and Atlantic. Also, all political decisions in the NATO council, which is preceded by the -- which is presided by the secretary-general, are translated by the military committee into guidance into supreme allied commanders Europe and Atlantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: But I should say the chairman is not in the chain of command. It's one of the peculiars in an organisation such as NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this first meeting on October 15th?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, it -- it was a direct consequence of Mr. Holbrooke's negotiations with the late Mr. Milosevic. Holbrooke, as you may remember, came back from these meetings with Milosevic in, I think it was on the 12th and 13th of October, 1998. He reported on certain progress he had made in the political arena, and he asked NATO to agree on the so-called activation order, the ACTORD.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is an ACTORD?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The activation order means that from this moment on -- when the act is agreed, the secretary-general of NATO is entitled to use the forces which are described in the activation order without asking the nations for further political agreement. So at this moment he has the key to use force in -- it's a delegation of the NATO nations to the secretary-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was anyone else with you, other than Clark and Solana?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Michael Durkee, the -- I think the American's call it the POLA, the Political Advisor of Supreme Allied Commander Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he worked for General Clark?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: He worked for General Clark, but please don't ask my whether he is working on a NATO bullet or an American national bullet. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We had -- of course, we had a couple of our collaborators with us, but they were not part of the discussions which took place with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You tell us in your -- your written evidence at paragraph 4 that General Perisic and Mr. Milutinovic were present with Mr. Milosevic during that four- or five-hour meeting on the 15th of October. Were both of them present when you, Clark, and Solana warned Mr. Milosevic about the use of disproportionate force against ethnic Albanians and that it had to stop in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were -- they both were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were those conversations in English, or were they being translated?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The entire conversation took place in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did General Perisic speak English?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I suspect he was able to understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: But he did not speak -- yes. He spoke English, since in -- at a later meeting we were sitting in his office and he spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I -- as far as I recall, Mr. Milutinovic speaks fluent English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You say in these discussions that you, NATO representatives, presented some evidence to Mr. Milosevic about what NATO considered excess deployment of MUP or police and VJ forces in Kosovo. And in your transcript at page 6969 beginning at line 22, you mention that the numbers of police units and the numbers of VJ units. In that particular paragraph, does "numbers" refer to how many police officers and soldiers there were, or are you referring to unit identifiers?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We -- I think we covered in this discussion both. We covered unit identifiers; and when we spoke of total personnel strength, we spoke of deployed police officers or deployed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P454 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next meeting, General, I'd like to show you a document and see if you can tell us what that is. It may take a moment to come up on your screen. Now, I see that appears to be a French version.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No problem, I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, perhaps. And one more -- I thought I had an English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I apologise, General. I think I've identified the wrong number. I'll try and locate the English later. Oh, okay. Now I see something. I don't know if you've seen this document before or not. Would you like us to scroll down to the document of the page?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I've seen this document before, but not in the court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It's a verification agreement which General Clark and, I believe, General Perisic or the Minister of Defence of the former Yugoslav -- of the former Yugoslavia had worked out in -- more or less in -- in the execution of the Holbrooke agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And was this something that was discussed with or arrived at during that October 15th visit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was not discussed in detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then move on to the next meeting. You returned to Belgrade on the 24th and 25th of October, 1998, according to your prior evidence?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened to cause you to go back so soon?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the NATO council had decided to send us back to more or less deliver a last warning to the Yugoslav leadership, to respond to the requests of NATO to reduce the excess police and military force in Kosovo, and to explain, if I may say so, to Mr. Milosevic and his team which authorities NATO was given with the activation order and what this could mean for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess you may have answered my next question already. Why were you and Clark chosen for this job?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: There was a long discussion in NATO about this. The NATO council came to the conclusion that it might be -- it might add additional credibility to the, if I may say so, the ultimatum which NATO was about to deliver if two military officers came and explained to the Yugoslav leadership what the activation order could mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us in simple terms, I guess, what was the nature of the ultimatum that you and Clark were going to give to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Following the habits of military, we used, I should say, straightforward language and told Mr. Milosevic that within 48 hours NATO could bomb the former Yugoslav republic, unless we saw a tangible and verifiable reduction of the deployment of additional forces to Kosovo and an end to hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him the existence of an activation order and what that meant?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, he -- Mr. Milosevic was fully aware that the activation order existed. I think he was aware when we met on the 15th of October that the activation order was agreed. And I also believe, at least according to what Mr. Solana told me, in debriefing me on his bilateral with Mr. Milosevic, at which I was not present and Clark was not present, he explained to Mr. Milosevic what the activation order means and what the consequence of noncompliance could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your transcript at page 6977, beginning at line 9, you tell us that you and Clark arrived in Belgrade. You met with Ambassador Miles and Shaun Byrnes from US-KDOM, and then you met to a meeting at Bijeli Dvori, the white palace. Who else was there from the NATO side? Was Mike Durkee there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mike Durkee was there as well and some of my collaborators. In my case, I was accompanied by my military assistant Colonel Bischof [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention on page 6993 at line 7 of your transcript and paragraph 26 of your interview notes that at this meeting Mr. Sainovic was introduced to you as "the man responsible for Kosovo." Do you recall who introduced him to you in that capacity? Who said that about him?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was Mr. Milosevic himself who introduced him in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that said in English?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this the first time you had met Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So he had not been at the 15th October meeting, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. At paragraphs 12 and 13 of your notes of your OTP interview, you -- you tell how you as a group explained to Mr. Milosevic that the only way to avoid NATO intervention was to reduce the numbers of police and VJ in Kosovo and to stop the use of disproportionate force versus the civilian population. And you told him he only had 48 hours in which to accomplish that. Who had set the deadline of 48 hours, and what did that relate to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The deadline of 48 hours was set by the NATO council. And, of course, if you try to understand the situation as it existed then, the NATO nations were running a little bit out of patience. They had threatened again and again that they might use force in order to enforce an end of hostilities, but to no -- there was no result. And so they eventually decided, Okay, we will issue an ultimatum, and that was our task to deliver this message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your written evidence at paragraph 18 and in your transcript at page 6973 and 697 -- well, 6973 at line 2 and on, you describe the efforts that you all went to to try and hammer out some sort of agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P395. This is already in evidence, Your Honour. And in connection with the transcript, our Exhibit 395 is the same as Milosevic Exhibit 94, tab 3, which is referred to at page 6985, line 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So after spending the night, basically, you went back with the next morning and had an agreement to be signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document that's on the screen now, General?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. I recognise this document very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is your name on that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can scroll down and look at the rest of the signatures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. My name is down on the left bottom side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see all the other people who signed at that time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whose signature is that with no signature block?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is the signature of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you describe in your evidence --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think I described how it came about and why we insisted on him to sign this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is my question. Why were you and General Clark so insistent that he be a signer?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, based on all we had learned in our involvement in this Kosovo crisis, and Clark of course earlier on in the -- during his involvement in the Dayton negotiations, we knew that -- well, our assessment was that an agreement had only a chance to be executed and implemented if it was personally accepted by Mr. Milosevic. And for that reason, we insisted that he should sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness next Exhibit P394 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're moving to something else --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- there's a couple of things I would like to clarify about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back to the 48-hour question, is 48 hours the period it would take to actually activate the ACTORD or does it relate to something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The reaction time, if you mean this, Your Honour, the reaction time would have been shorter than 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was the 48-hour period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- we had seen the number of forces which were in the province of Kosovo, and we had made let's say an estimate how long it would take to restore these forces, since we didn't want to impose anything on the Yugoslav side which was not possible to be executed. And so we said 48 hours should be sufficient to redeploy these forces from Kosovo to Serbia proper; and for this purpose, the 48 hours had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that period mentioned at the meeting on the 24th of October or had it arisen on the 15th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was the first time mentioned on the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just the way that it's phrased here it says "You have had 48 hours to deliver," which doesn't sound as though it's an accurate reflection of what had happened. It's sounds as if you're saying you have 48 hours to deliver.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We said at the meeting on the 24th, Your Honour, you have 48 hours to deliver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 which follows that paragraph 12, you say that you told Milosevic of the contents of a report about the shelling of a village with artillery. Can you recollect which village that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I can't recollect. I know that I got the information on the flight to Belgrade, and it was corroborated NATO intelligence at the time. And for that reason, I mentioned it as an example for disproportionate response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sort of information would come to you from which sources? I don't require you to be specific. It's just the nature of the sources I'm anxious to establish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact source, but NATO depends in its intelligence on the information provided by the member nations. A member nation reports without telling us whether this is -- us is NATO, without telling NATO whether this is the result of human intelligence or technical intelligence or overhead imagery. But the habit is also that we never believe in one nation reporting alone. We then ask others whether they have similar information. Only when we have the corroboration by another nation, we accept it as a NATO-agreed intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would evidence of the shelling of a village include evidence from human sources who had been passing their personal experience to NATO members, and would it also include overhead imagery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If overhead imagery would have been able to detect the shelling of a village, it would include it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was to be my main question here. How do you detect that a village has been shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you have, I should say, a wider way of human intelligence available. You may have people on the ground. You may have diplomatic observers. At this time the KDOM was in the country. You may also get information by the one or the other citizen living in this area telling the KDOM people, Look, this happened. And in the one or the other case, we might see indications for shelling on overhead imagery, but it's not necessarily the case that we -- that we could monitor all villages and cities in Kosovo with overhead imagery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with that report in paragraph 13 you say, It was possible that Perisic might not have yet been aware of this because it was -- it had only just occurred. So this was a fresh incident.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was, as I had stated earlier on, it was given to us during the flight to Belgrade as an incident which had happened. And when I say in my statement that it might be possible that Mr. Perisic didn't know about it, I referred to the experience gained in my own military life that not all information on a single evidence is immediately brought to the attention of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then Judge Bonomy's earlier question in paragraph 12 at the bottom of page 3, it's quoted as Mr. Milosevic was being told. "Mr. President, the hammer is cocked, the clock is ticking, and you have had 48 hours to deliver." Is it your testimony that should read "and you have 48 hours to deliver?"

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that would be more correct, since we already told him it's -- we still have 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 394 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to this statement you just saw on the screen you signed and Mr. Milosevic signed, among others, were there additional agreements reached over this weekend of the 24th and 25th?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: There was an agreement -- an additional agreement on the number of check-points, which I think Mr. Shaun Byrnes had worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Exhibit 394 on the screen, Your Honours, is the Milosevic exhibit 94, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this the document you were referring to, General?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P432?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you know who -- I'm not sure if I'm pronouncing it right, Mr. Geremek or Jovanovic are? This is on a document to come up.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In a moment.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I know who Geremek is. He was the Polish Minister of Foreign Affairs and Jovanovic was the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the former republic Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have heard an agreement that's referred to sometimes as the Geremek/Jovanovic agreement. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was the verification of the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen that agreement before?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I have seen the agreement before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does this document on the screen appear to be that screen?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One more, General, before I move on to some other questions, and I think this may be the English version of what I asked you about earlier. P440, if we could have that on the screen. This appears to be a cover letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. That is the Clark, I think, Perisic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that related to the aerial surveillance?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: To the aerial surveillance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that entered into before this weekend, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was, to the best of my recollection, worked out on the 15th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: So before the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 25 of your interview notes and at page 6991 of your testimony, you describe an incident after that agreement was signed with Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Djordjevic, yourself, and Clark, when Mr. Milosevic said words to the effect that it would -- that a solution to the Kosovo problem would be found in the spring. Can you tell the Court what you recall about how that came up. It's described in your written evidence, but if you can tell us today what you remember.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was after we had asked Mr. Milosevic to sign the agreement, which we had worked out throughout the night, and then Mr. Milosevic offered us a form of drink. In the earlier proceedings, I learned it was not slivovitz as was my recollection, but it was some form of peach brandy. But I'm definitely not an expert on alcohol, so you may forgive me this slight incorrectness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think, previously, he said pear brandy, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I don't know. It was -- whether it was pear or peach, I don't know. Anyway, I think it's not so important. The -- then he mentioned, more or less in passing and a little bit as a surprise to all of us, that he was really determined to find a solution to this problem with the Kosovars, which he did not call with -- in a very friendly way. He used words like "murderers," "bandits," "rapists," and to the best of my recollection, he said, I'll find a final solution in spring next year or spring 1999. And you can imagine what the word "final solution" means for a German. I got a little bit -- really, a little bit nervous and he said -- I asked him, What do you mean by "final solution"? And he said, We'll do to them what we did to them in, I think he said in 1946 in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know what he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No, I had no idea. I -- it's -- I have often stated, thereafter, that it was one of our biggest -- one of our mistakes in western Europe that we did not look into the history of this part of Europe. Also, it was so close to our doorsteps. So I didn't know, and we asked and he explained to us. And if I recall it properly, he said it was quite simple. We got them all together and we shot them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you and Clark were present when this was said. Who else was there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was -- but I'm not entirely sure. It could also be that Mike Durkee was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the Serb side, anyone else?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: On the Serb side I believe it was General Djordjevic, Mr. Milutinovic, not so -- not entirely sure whether it was Mr. Sainovic, but I could imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was there any reaction from those who heard this comment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No, no reaction which I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No one said anything?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was, in most cases, their usual attitude that they did not say anything when Mr. Milosevic spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unless they were asked to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a page in the transcript for this subject which --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think page 6991 is where it's discussed. I can double-check. Yeah, beginning I think at line -- line 8 as a good starting point. Does Your Honour find that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have found it. Do you have your -- or does the General have in front of him the interview notes of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- 17th of June and then proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look, please, Mr. Naumann, at paragraph 24 of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where someone has recorded -- where I think you claim were the actual words used, the parts in quotation marks. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, is my recollection of this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the interpretation has recorded your recollection rather differently today on the transcript, and I'm wondering if there is some misunderstanding in today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I scroll back the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what it says. You're quoted as saying that he said: "I'll find a final solution. And you can imagine what the word 'final solution' meant for a German."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that doesn't appear in this statement, and it doesn't appear in the Milosevic transcript either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, it was eight years ago and I believe and I don't know why I didn't mention it then. I believe he said a"final solution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's such a striking thing at this minute. It appears quite surprising that you wouldn't have mentioned it earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I mentioned it and I overlooked it when I got the written documentation of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the cross-examination by Milosevic, the issue arose over whether there had been any earlier reference made by you or Clark to this, and there was some discussion of Clark's book. One of the unfortunate features of this whole business is that everybody involved seems to have written a book. Have you written one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's reassuring. But so far as you personally are concerned, had you ever on any earlier occasion raised this comment anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had given, Your Honour, a speech in, I think in fall 1999 [Realtime transcript read in error "4/1999"] at the German General Staff and Command College in Hamburg reflecting on my experiences in this Kosovo crisis and the lessons learned from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that? Sorry, I think we've got the wrong date here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in fall 1999. Not 4, fall, autumn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the report back of the events that had occurred? Was this not something that was reported to NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reported this when we -- when we came back. We reported it to the secretary-general orally. And we also reported in the NATO council orally that we gave the impression that the crisis was not over with this agreement, and a solution to the Kosovar problem was about to be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were the terms of this conversation, though, not reported back to NATO specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the terms of the conversation were reported to the secretary-general, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that report to him an oral report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was an oral report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just you and Clark?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, and the head of the private office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who would that be, or can you say?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was a Spaniard called Domek [phoen], family name Domek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So after this agreement was signed, you returned to Brussels. And at page 6994, line 4 and following, and page -- or paragraph 28 of your notes, you tell us you returned to Brussels, you reported on what had happened, the decision was made to not implement the ACTORD at that time. And as a matter of fact, the Serbs initially complied and withdrew how many policemen? 6.000?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Somewhere between 5.000 and 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But then you tell us at page 6995, beginning at line 15, you note the compliance didn't last for too long, and that as of November you saw again reports of violations. Can you tell us what was the nature of the violations that were being reported? Did it have to do with the numbers of forces present in Kosovo, or did it have to do with disproportionate force being used?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was both. We saw disproportionate use of force, we saw establishment, I think, of additional check-points, and we saw some redeployments. But in most cases - and I think I have stated this before - the incidents were not triggered by the Yugoslav side. They were triggered by the Albanian side or the Kosovar side, who tried to explore -- take advantage of the vacuum left by the Serb side, who had withdrawn in accordance with the agreement; and then they moved in, in some cases acting rather provocatively as indicating that this was part of the -- of a Republic of Kosovo or something like this. And the Serb side reacted to that, I think in a way which -- the reaction as such was understandable to us. What was not understandable to us was from time to time the way in which they reacted. So we saw -- we were suddenly again in a spirit of force and counter-force which was military reinforcing and led to escalation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was it about the way in which they reacted that you found not understandable?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, we -- it was -- as we have often seen and often said in these various conversations, it was a heavy-handed approach in which they used ways and means in response to unrest, which was not in -- which we simply did not know from our countries. We -- when we had a terrorist activity or a criminal activity, we tried to respond to that by using police forces, but not by moving in military or paramilitary forces which were using relevant brute force to suppress unrest. And that, I think, disproportionality was again and again a fact we had to note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the extent of the terrorist threat here, though, not a much greater one than other western European nations have experienced in their own domestic circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was different from the terrorist threat which we have seen in other European countries, perhaps with the exception of the situation in Northern Ireland and in the Basque part of Spain. And, for instance, what we had seen in my country were terrorist activities were -- were nothing like this. In our case there were terrorist acts against individuals, but never the attempt to more or less be in control of a part of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The various agreements that had been reached, though, left or provided for no avenue to deal with the KLA. Now, was there any NATO plan as to how the KLA might be dealt with in the environment you were trying to create, which was an environment of mediation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, was our Achilles' heel, if I can say this. We had made a -- I'm saying this quite openly and bluntly, and I hope straightforward -- in a straightforward way. We had made a mistake. We, I mean the political leadership of NATO in spring 1998 when we called the KLA a group of terrorists. That you find in NATO documents like the foreign ministers' meeting. And having stated that the KLA is a group of terrorists, we had I think inadvertently paralyzed our own instrument to cope with them, since in NATO was the -- there is no -- there was never any hope at all to contact terrorists directly. You need -- for a decision, you need for the consensus of, at this time 16 nations. And since some of the nations had a terrorist problem at their hands, they simply and flatly refused that we should ever talk to terrorists. And that was our Achilles' heel. We had simply no instrument to rein-in the KLA. We had to do it. We tried to do it by asking the one or the other NATO nation to take advantage of contacts which may exist. But the instrument which we used in the case of the Yugoslavs; namely, to threaten military action, was not applicable to the Kosovars. That was our -- our mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, just before I forget, this is something quite distinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 22 where you're dealing with the various documents, and one is the Clark-Naumann-Milosevic-Djordjevic-Sainovic agreement, that that was made up of two parts. There was a statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- which contained a detail. Does that have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's all part of Exhibit 440, I think you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's 395, so are there two numbers for that combined document or is it all 395.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 395 contains both the signature page and the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, if I understand then, part of the problem, as you see it, is because NATO has earlier declared KLA a terrorist group. By NATO's own rules, then you couldn't negotiate with them or have discussions with them?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct. We had to ask nations, individual nations, to contact them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I could just check something on the transcript to an answer you gave earlier at page 31, line 19, I think I heard something differently than was recorded on the transcript. And you were talking about how you tried to respond in your country to terrorist activity with police forces, and not by moving in military or paramilitary forces which was using relevant brute force. I thought I heard you say "relatively brute force?"

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Relatively brute force, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is an example of the relatively brute force you saw in Kosovo by the Serbs against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We saw it occasionally, and I think we mentioned it to our Serb interlocutors that they moved a tank company in front of a village, started to shell the village, and then went in. And that is something which I think is disproportionate, if you deal with unrest of a -- let's say of a terrorist nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you had a lot of experience in your military career with the artillery; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's fair to say, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if you have an incident, say, of a single sniper shooting at a police convoy or a group of military convoys --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- what's the appropriate response?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If you have an individual sniper, you try to take out the sniper at the maximum, by using, let's say, an APC gun or an individual tank, but you never move -- you move use an entire company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, as a result of this information you were getting in November/December of 1998 about non-compliance, you made a third trip to Belgrade to see Mr. Milosevic on the 19th of January --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- 1999. Who went besides you and General Clark on this third trip?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The -- on our side, the composition was more or less the same, but in Belgrade we met Ambassador Walker, who was then the head of the OSCE verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had he been declared persona non grata at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Before that point, he had been declared a persona non grata, yes, because he had spoken up in the Racak event in a way which, as Mr. Milosevic later explained to us, was very and utterly unacceptable to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So who went to see Milosevic, you and Clark and Mike Durkee, was he along on this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else as you recall? Was your aid with you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: He was sitting in the anteroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was there on the Serb side with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think, again, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think in your written evidence, you mentioned another individual who took notes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. A man who was in the personal staff of Mr. Milosevic, I think Bugarcic or something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 36 of your statement and at page 7007 beginning at line 11, you tell us that you guys told Milosevic about the excess numbers of police being brought back into Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- about disproportionate use of force by both police and military, and about armoured units being outside of their garrison. And you said, in connection with this, you gave Mr. Milosevic a list of you think it was ten incidents of violations. We're still trying, as I said, to locate that list. Do you recall any of the incidents that were on that list?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We had -- this was a list which had been established in NATO headquarters, and in which we really had picked the most significant incidents and violations which we had seen or NATO intelligence had seen in the time-frame December to January 1999. So we had -- we had more, but in the intelligence files. But we had picked I think there were ten or so incidents and listed them, since they were really examples of, in our view, clear-cut violations of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was Racak on that list, or was that a separate item?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Racak was I think -- was on -- I think it was on the list, but please don't name me down on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about Podujevo in December 1998, do you recall if that was on the list?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Podujevo I think was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what that incident was about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I've -- I have to admit, it's a rather faint recollection. I think it was, again, a disproportionate use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 39 of your notes, there are transcribed some of your handwritten notes from that last meeting in January 1999, and you mentioned that issues discussed included ICTY, OSCE, and HOM. Can you tell us what HOM stands for in that context.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's the KVM --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was the head of mission, Mr. Walker, since we wanted to make -- we tried to persuade Mr. Milosevic that Ambassador Walker should stay in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's another note farther down called compliance. "Not one incident triggered by MUP/VJ reacted 25 October agreement." Do you recall what that was about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's -- it reflects what I had stated earlier on, that the incidents were in -- triggered by the KLA and not by the Yugoslav armed forces were, for which VJ stands, and the police was, for which MUP stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the source of your information for that, that not one incident had been triggered by MUP or VJ?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that NATO information?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It was information primarily based on observations by the OSCE verifiers and the KDOM people who were still to some extent operating independently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not pausing for the interpreters. There was a note: "Will not comply on ICTY and not now in compliance." Do you recall what that referred to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. ICTY -- we had asked to admit Judge Arbour, who was waiting in Skopije and Macedonia, to enter Yugoslavia and to -- to start an independent inquiry on the Racak event. And my notes there simply say we will not indicate -- he refused to admit Judge Arbour to come to Yugoslavia, so he does not agree on the involvement of the ICTY. And I think "not in noncompliance" I think that refers to, in my impression - and that was my note - the former Republic of Yugoslavia was not in compliance with the 25 October agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was the last time you met with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was the last time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. No, sorry. I met Mr. Milosevic here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. I guess I forget about that as being a meeting. General, I think the rest of your evidence is in your written materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions at this time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Naumann, in these various notes you've made, there is reference to a heading "Compliance, not one incident triggered by MUP or VJ." And then it goes on: "Admitted not to be in compliance but expressed desire to gradually return to it in step-by-step approach, no chance now since Podujevo increasingly ethnically cleansed." Now, is that a reference to something that happened at the 25th of October meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have -- I think my notes reflect my impression that the Serb side expressed they might return to the 25 October agreement over time, but they needed a little bit more time in -- in order to cope with the situation, as they saw it. But the reference to Podujevo indicates that they -- that they also had started a process of -- well, what we called ethnic cleansing of some villages. And the numbers, which I think were given to us, were that 18 villages had already been more or less cleansed and -- or cleaned. And the total of villages was 72. That's my recollection of this note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if this happened on the 19th of January, it's inconsistent with what you've said about Milosevic's attitude, which was to deny that there were any breaches or that there was any responsibility, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see -- I don't see the inconsistency, Your Honour. He denied that there was any misbehaving on the side of the Serb military or police force in the Racak event and accused us of having used force information when we talked about Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But this idea of -- that from the Serb side came a desire to gradually return to compliance in a step-by-step approach is surely inconsistent with the attitude you were experiencing from Milosevic, which was to deny that there was any disproportionate use of force and to deny that the forces were in any way acting inappropriately. But -- and to explain that the increase in troop movement was necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- again, with all due respect, I do not see the inconsistency. We -- if you looked at the final paragraph of the so-called Naumann-Clark agreement where we talk about the right of self-defence, then you find the key to the solution of your observation. We had accepted in this final paragraph the right of self-defence, which is quite normal and understandable for every state, but we obviously had a -- I should say a different interpretation of what proportionality means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand -- I think you misunderstand my question, Mr. Naumann. It's -- your statement in your note"admitted not to be in compliance," now who admitted noncompliance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what my note says is that he admitted the noncompliance in terms of numbers, since there were more forces in Kosovo than it was stated in the 25 October agreement. We -- but we had not any agreement at all on the question of proportionality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- the other matter I want to ask is this: The -- I know that February was occupied partially by negotiations which ultimately failed, but there's a leap in your account of events from the 19th of January directly to the 23rd of March and a decision to take action. Was the decision actually taken around the 19th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what was it then that triggered the decision on the 23rd of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gap in my account is, I think, explainable since after -- more or less after Racak the decision -- the political decision was taken that NATO should no longer be in the driving seat, but the contact group, the new established contact group should take the lead. And this led to the negotiations of Rambouillet and Paris in which NATO did not participate. We were kept informed, but we had no responsibility whatsoever for the contents of these negotiations. When the negotiations failed - and I think the final moment of failure was the last visit of Ambassador Holbrooke to Belgrade on the 23rd of March - then NATO came again into the game. But we were left with no option, so we simply had to execute after the politics had failed to achieve a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm really trying to find out is whether there was another assessment made of the situation within the former Yugoslavia before ultimately a decision was made to carry out the threat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a -- Your Honour, this was a process of permanent assessment, and of course the NATO council was -- remained involved in discussions -- discussing of the situation. But as I tried to say, they were not in the driving seat at this time, which by the way was not extremely helpful in terms of maintaining the coalition of the alliance and the contact group, which contained at the time four NATO nations; namely, United States, United Kingdom, France, and Germany, and as a non-NATO nation Russia. The establishment of this group had triggered quite a series of not always pleasant discussions among the allies, since the one or the other failed to be an underprivileged member. So they -- the noncontact group members still had to contribute to the execution of an eventual decision to use force in Kosovo. So we had I think some rifts in the -- in the alliance at this point in time, but we continued to -- to look into the situation of -- in the former Yugoslavia, and it was not as if we had a pause of, let's say, six weeks. But we were not actively involved in the discussions. We had tried, I can also say. We had tried to be involved. Since we knew had there been a peaceful agreement at Rambouillet or Paris, NATO would have been asked to take on some elements of the implementation. But there was no agreement -- no political agreement that NATO should be involved, and so we couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumann. It's a convenient time for us to have our break, which we have to have. So could you, while we have the break, go with the usher, and we shall see you when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing in the transcript, I believe 39 -- page 39, 24, it says: "And accused us of having used force information." I actually think that the witness said "false information." That is the only thing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We will resume at 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the order of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lukic, and Mr. Milutinovic. [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The first counsel to cross-examine will be Mr. Sepenuk on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, as Judge Bonomy said, I'm Norman Sepenuk and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, I want to start with what you said on June 7th, 2000, when you were testifying before the House of Commons Defence Select Committee as part of its inquiry into the lessons of Kosovo. And that by the way -- what you said is in Defence Exhibit 3D777, and if I can just read it to you, sir. You said: "I think it is fair to say that Milosevic honoured the commitment which he had made to General Clark and myself on October 25, 1998. He withdrew the forces and he withdrew the police. There may have been some difference as to whether there were 200 or 400 policemen more or less, but that does not really matter. More or less, he honoured the commitment, then the UJK [sic] or KLA filled the void, the withdrawn Serb forces had left, and they escalated. I have stated this in the NATO council in October and November repeatedly. In most cases, the escalation came from the Kosovar side, not from the Serb side." And I take it, sir, that you remember those words and those are indeed your words? You have to answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I remember these words, and I think that is also in line with what I said earlier on when I was asked more or less in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. And, General, since you were not on the ground yourself in Kosovo, I take it you were not on the ground in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I also take it that based -- that you based your statement, the one I've just read, for example, on reports that you received from those on the ground, and as I understand it, initially from KDOM and later from the Kosovo Verification Mission. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And at the Milosevic trial you stated that during November and December of 1998, there were again reports of violations of the cease-fire agreement by both Serb and KLA forces, yes?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that in the Milosevic trial at page 6995, you stated as follows, with respect to this November/December period. You said: "I should really say in all fairness to the best information I got from the reports on the ground from KDOM, and later on from the Kosovo verification regime, many of the incidents were triggered by the UCK, who obviously tried to exploit the vacuum created by the withdrawn Serb security forces and who then sneaked in to take control of regions or areas. They also, I think, launched provocations and they were not free of violence doing that." Is that -- that was your testimony, I take it, in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And, General, as the year 1998 drew to a close, is it fair to say - and I'm picking up on something that Judge Bonomy asked you a little while ago - is it fair to say that neither the OSCE nor NATO nor Ambassador Hill, nor anybody else for that matter, had been successful in successfully stopping KLA provocations?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, that was my impression at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is it also fair to say that the prospect of KLA provocations in the future was even more likely considering that it was common knowledge, at least at this time, December 1998, it was common knowledge that the KLA was threatening to kill any Albanian who signed any agreements negotiated by US-KDOM Ambassador Hill. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That I cannot remember, in that clarity as you just stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
