utterances.text: The reason I asked you that is we had a witness here General Drewienkiewicz, who I take it you know. Do you know General DZ?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't know General DZ?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General Drewienkiewicz, does that ring a bell? He was the number three man --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That was the British database.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: British guy --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: British general who was a deputy in the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Exactly. He was the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Now I remember his nickname, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Which was what just for the heck of it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: DZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He testified here and he submitted a statement that said precisely that, that it was public at the time - this is December 1998 - that the KLA was threatening to kill anyone who signed any agreements with Ambassador Hill. But that was not in your frame of knowledge; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Correct. And I should also say in all fairness to use his own words, that they never reported in such clarity to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And by the end of the year, the prospects of the KLA limiting their provocations became even more remote when the KLA declared "1999 as the year of independence for Kosovo." Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I do not remember that they quoted this at the end of 1999, but it was their aim all the time. That is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That their aim --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And it is today by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it was certainly back then, independence for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then moving into early January 1999, I want to ask you a series of questions - and I'm going to bring you January until the time the war started - to determine your knowledge of the -- of your source, I should say. I think earlier today you stated, at least right before the break, you stated page 37, lines 22, 23, the source of your information that an -- as to whether an incident had been triggered by the MUP or the VJ, were the OSCE verifiers and KDOM, who was still operating effectively in the field. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So what I want to do is go to those sources and see how much you really knew in reaching a conclusion about -- the conclusions you've reached; disproportionate use of force and that kind of thing. I want to be able to determine whether the extent of your knowledge concerning KLA provocations, so we can determine the reasonableness of a conclusion you reached about disproportionate use of force. And I'm asking you this, General, with respect because you were a very high figure, a four-star general at the very top, a very exulted position. And I want to see how much you were in touch with those people on the ground. You may have been very closely in touch, but that is going to be the point of my questions. All right, sir? I would like to go to the beginning of the year. We've talked about November/December, and I want to go to 2 January 1999. We can put any of these up on the screen, if you would like or the Prosecutor would like or anybody else, but I will read from the exhibit. I have the assessment from 2 January 1999 and this is the KVM --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a reference to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution Exhibit 407, page 100. If you could put that up on the screen, please. No, that's not it. P407, 100. It's from the blue book, the Prosecution blue book. We just checked this again last night, so I think we're right on this or else heads will role, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P407.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Well, at this point I'd like to -- do you have that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mine says assessment 2 January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That was not what they first put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, General?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this is the assessment of the KVM fusion centre. "There are indications that KLA may be coming more closely unified under a centralised command structure. Units of the KLA are now being identified to KVM patrols by specific unit designation. Areas of responsibility are being adjusted by the KLA, and loosely affiliated groups may be coming under centralised control." Now, do you remember receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I remember receiving similar reports; similar, but not exactly this wording, since you should understand the mechanics in NATO headquarters. When I got the information presented, it was the condensed, corroborated information, which did not only refer to one source but to a couple of sources. But the gist of it, that is, the information I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Just to take -- this is January 2nd, 1999. Just to take a very brief diversion here, we have a document, and I'll read from that document and put it up on the screen if necessary. It's Prosecution Exhibit 2460, and what it is, General, is a report by Colonel Bislim Zyrapi. Do you know who he is, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't know who Bislim Zyrapi is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I can assure you the name was never mentioned at any NATO intelligence briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well for your information, sir, he was the Chief of the General Staff of the KLA beginning in November 1998, held that position through April. He had a rather responsible position with the KLA, but I take it, again, you don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And I can -- this is in line with what I said earlier on, we had no contacts with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But, certainly, you felt it your duty to learn as much about the KLA as possible, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: About their intentions, capabilities, yes, but not necessarily the personalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you had KLA liaisons from OSCE and KDOM out in the field with the KLA did you not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The OSCE had contacts with the KLA as well as KDOM, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So getting back to that exhibit, that's a report of the General Staff as of December 28th, 1998, just a few days before this January 1999 assessment, which talked about becoming more closely unified. And in this report on page 2, it says and -- actually page 3, it says: "Following the enemy offensive," and what he's referring to is the offensive of the Serb forces that culminated in the October 1998 agreement. "Following the enemy offensive, the re-positioning of forces," that means repositioning of KLA forces, "has been carried out in all operative zones. And we can freely say that the territory controlled by our units is now of a greater percentage than prior to the enemy offensive." Does that jive with your recollection that at the beginning -- as of at least the end of the year, the KLA had moved into all of the positions vacated by the MUP and the VJ and, indeed, controlled even more of the country than before? Does that jive with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I would not confirm more, but that they had tried to fill the vacuum that was created by the withdrawal of the Serb forces from certain positions as negotiated in the 25 October agreement, that I had stated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then on page 4 of this statement, the -- Colonel Bislim Zyrapi goes on to say -- he's talking about proposals for the use of tactical and operational units for combat activities in the future. And he says: "The following proposals taken from the commander's written reports have been singled out." The first is: "Acting in commando groups in towns and inside the zones where the enemy is active, cutting out enemy supply lines through diversion actions, hitting everywhere the living enemy forces in order to inflict insecurity at all times and everywhere." Now, realising that you didn't get a copy of this report and you didn't deal with Colonel Zyrapi, did your NATO intelligence sources or your KVM or KDOM sources essentially convey to you the gist of what I just read, that the KLA was ready to attack anywhere at any time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, as I had stated, Mr. Sepenuk, earlier on, I had the impression that in most cases the incidents were triggered by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, can we have an exhibit number for that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, that was 24 -- that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I have it 2460.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: 2460. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you did give us it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: At any point -- there's going to be a number more exhibits. If it would clarify anything, I would be happy to put it on the screen, but I didn't think there would be any dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Going back to the January 2nd assessment, General, which is right before you. It says: "An interesting trend is developing with the VJ becoming more cooperative with the OSCE and its operation, and the KLA becoming more belligerent and uncooperative at their security positions. There are also indications that the KLA is becoming more firm in their goal of a totally independent Kosovo." And letting your memory wander back to early 1999, General, did you receive this kind of information? Is this consistent with what you recall about that period?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That -- what I recall, Mr. Sepenuk, is that we came to the conclusion that the KLA is more active than the VJ and the MUP were at this time, that they were trying to seize the initiative. Of course, the political objective of gaining independence, that I had stated earlier on. That was something which was printed in all papers more or less every day. But I couldn't fully confirm that we had a full agreement in NATO that this was really the -- I should say the common assessment shared by all nations in the alliance. We presented the situation I think in a very similar way, since after all most of the bases for our information were the OSCE reports, the verification mission reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what I read to you was apparently the KVM assessment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then just jumping ahead --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did these reports come to you or come to NATO direct, or did they come to you through the member states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The -- we had an agreement with the OSCE that we got the reports directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And jumping ahead about a week to January 8th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, again, I would ask the usher to put up P407, page 156. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, what you have before you is, again, a KVM assessment for 8 January 1999, and it talks about a well-executed ambush against a MUP patrol near Suva Reka. And I can tell you that during that ambush three MUP were killed, three members of the police were killed and a number wounded. And it states that it validates the KLA's earlier threats to retaliate against MUP patrols and VJ check-points; and then it says: "It appears the KLA does not acknowledge the cease-fire anymore and will most likely strike again using the same tactics." Now, again, did this information get to you that in effect in substance the KLA was not really acknowledging the cease-fire, and they weren't a party to any agreement and they didn't acknowledge the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Again, I should say, Mr. Sepenuk, not in this rather general and generalising way. The assessment was presented to NATO. We had information that occasionally and in -- on the one or the other occasion, one could come to the conclusion that the KLA would no longer acknowledge the cease-fire; but then, as it is also by the way written the same assessment, the Serb side reacted by establishing an additional check-point. So we had this spiral of escalation and counter-escalation, and it was a spiral of mutually reinforcing violence. In many cases. It was simply not possible to identify who kicked it off and who reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as you point out, General, in that report it says there was another check-point established; however, once the check-point was established, the KLA seized this as an opportunity to conduct another strike. The subsequent assault by the KLA on this check-point indicates the KLA's high level of confidence and willingness to attack in multiple locations. And is that something that also -- I'm talking about the level of confidence now. We're talking about an organisation that shown -- that showed virtually no inclination not to use violence; correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Again, I should say don't take such an example as the general picture throughout the province. This -- incidents like this happened, that's true, and that's correctly described here, but there were other parts where it was exactly the other way around. And I have the impression of these assessments that they are to some extent rather on point events, and some of the assessments generalise a local event as the description of the situations throughout the province, which is not entirely the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, rather than comment on that - and thank you for your comment - I think the point might be clarified by the next exhibit which is 3D473.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document should be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It has been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is not one that appears on the list of documents I have from you. There's a -- there is a 3D374, but not 473.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We can put this -- yeah. I think I should move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This is a press release and it's called: "Irresponsible acts by the OSCE," and it's called: "Irresponsible acts by the KLA." It talks about generally meticulously planned ambush, that we have already spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this 473? I don't have a copy of this. This hasn't been released to us, I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's in the system, and, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not one that we received notification was going to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It was my understanding that it had been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what do you want us to do, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to see a copy of it for one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, it is on the screen? You found it? Okay. Right. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the last paragraph of this, General, as you'll notice -- actually, the next-to-last paragraph says: "These actions," meaning this ambush by the KLA, "are in direct contradiction to solemn promises of the KLA of showing restraint and of maintaining the cease-fire agreement. KVM wishes to make it clear that it finds the reaction by Yugoslavian authorities to these KLA provocations has been up to this point very restrained. The representatives of the Yugoslavian authorities have shown a willingness to cooperate in the present situation." Now, that seems to me to be an overall comment about generally reactions to KLA provocations, at least that's my submission to you, and not just one little area. Do you disagree with that, General?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I do not disagree with that, but I should also point out this is an observation made public by the OSCE. And as we tried -- or as I tried to state earlier on and also in the Milosevic case when we presented President Milosevic with cases of disproportionate reaction on the Serb side, we also had examples which presumably could lead, if we take them together, to a similar conclusion just in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right, but I'm asking you now, sir - and I appreciate your comment - about specific documents and specific statements by the KVM. We could be here all day debating disproportionate use of force, et cetera. I'm asking you because of the limitations of time, I'm confining myself to specific documents here. And I'd like you next to look at Prosecution Exhibit 407, page 158.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Perhaps you can turn it around. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the last sentence of that, General, it's an assessment, KVM assessment for 8 January 1999 and it says: "The KLA appears to be taking advantage of OSCE's presence and becoming more provocative in their actions." Wasn't that really a correct view of things?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, it was -- it was a statement, Mr. Sepenuk, which I also heard in a similar way when we went to Belgrade in -- on the 19th of January, 1999. And as I said earlier on, you could easily make the case the other way around. But I admit, one could state it perhaps on this very day; and looking on this day on the incidents reported, the next day it could be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this is -- again, you say you heard it in Belgrade. This is not Mr. Milosevic speaking. This is the KVM; this is their statement.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I know, but I also would like to state that there could have been days, not the 8th of January, but perhaps 10th or 11th, what have you, in which the statement was exactly the other way around, putting the blame on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If there could have been -- I think Mr. Hannis will take care of it. Right now I want to deal with the now and the reality of what was going on then. And I'll show you another exhibit P407, page 345. And, General, you'll notice that says -- again, it's a significant events report for 26th January 1999, and it says: "Increased KLA activity. A patrol reports very strong KLA presence and a dramatic increase in the number of KLA fighters in the Prizren district. The KLA's police forces are manning numerous check-points, and KLA leaders expressed their concerns that they have -- are having difficulty holding back their fighters." Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Sepenuk, this corresponds exactly to what I stated earlier on when I said many of the incidents were triggered by the KLA also. I should add, if you look at the time-frame, this is the time-frame in which we were no longer in the driving seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. But you were still getting reports I gather?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We got reports but we were no longer in the driving seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No longer in the driving seat, but I'm, again, trying to assess the factual basis for some of your conclusions about disproportionate force. And I want to be able to show the Trial Chamber what the Serb forces were reacting against. That's the point of my question, sir. And turning to the assessment for 14 February 1999, it's 3D374. Okay. And if you would be kind enough to turn that around. Thank you. And, General, this is the KVM assessment for 14 February 1999, and they're talking about the military political situation and says that: "Even with the conduct of small-scale military and terrorist actions in the past several days, Kosovo has remained relatively quiet. The reason for this is probably due to the meeting in Rambouillet. Each side wanted to be seen as favouring peace in the region." Then it goes on to say: "On the same token, some of these incidents can be viewed as acts of provocation mainly by the KLA, trying to provoke reactionary operations by the other, which can then be exploited in the international arena." Is it fair to say that there was a general recognition that this was one of the goals of the KLA, to provoke -- to provoke reactions by the other side and get favourable treatment in the international arena. I take it you would agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I would not rule it out, but this was one of the intentions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then I have one or two other exhibits. The first one is 3D179. And this is -- General, this is a background report on compliance by the parties in Kosovo between the end of the Rambouillet talks and the beginning of the second Paris talks. And it covers the period 23 February to 11 March 1999, so we keep moving up here. And it says right in the first paragraph: "Unprovoked attacks by the KLA against the police have continued, and the number of casualties sustained by the security forces has increased." You notice that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. I notice that assessment. I also believe I remember it; but on the other hand, one should also note - and this is in the very same paragraph - that the number of deployed forces outside the barracks had been increased. So we are again back to this question of violence, triggering violence, and causing counter-violence. So it's -- I think it describes pretty fairly that both sides tried to jockey for influence in the international arena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Surely, General, is there any reason you looked over at the Prosecutor, sir, or do I have that wrong? You were looking over at Mr. Hannis. Did I have that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. I did not, sorry. I'm not getting instructions from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, I don't think you are. I think you're way above that. And surely, General, you don't mean to equate the Yugoslav units being out of barracks to attacks on Serb police and violations of the cease-fire, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I do not equate this, don't misunderstand me. But if you look at the situation in which both sides were - and I'm simply trying to understand both sides. I tried at the time and I'm doing it here again - the one side triggered an incident, the other sides reacts, perhaps a little bit clumsily; and then you go back into the next step of escalation. And that is the spiral I referred repeatedly to, which is obviously both sides were not able to get under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, again, I'm just trying to explore the factual basis for some of your conclusions. This report, by the way, General, contains numerous allegations, and I'm not sure there is time to go over it, but there are numerous allegations of cease-fire violations, killings of police, a number of those, a number of abductions of Serb civilians, a number of killings of Albanian-alleged collaborationists. Mr. Hannis can challenge this but I don't know he will, but the report is rife with that. I will ask you only one question regarding this, and that is on page 2 of that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher would turn to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It has -- and by the way before I dismiss, I'm trying to go through this with some dispatch, but didn't you become aware during this period that there were a number of abductions, killings, not only of security forces but of Serb civilians, killings of alleged Albanian collaborationists? Did this come to you in your position in NATO?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It came to me that we -- that a lot of killings on -- of Serb police officers took place, and I think I have stated this in my evidence which I gave to the Court, that some or other nasty events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Including Serb civilians and Albanian-alleged collaborationists?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Alleged collaborators, I did not state; and Serb civilians, I would also -- well, it's pretty difficult to clear-cut differentiate between a civilian and sometimes a policeman who is working in civilian clothes for police. But what I would -- I think the main point is that there was a lot of violence and cruelty committed by the Albanians towards Serbs in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And their fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That I could not -- I have no evidence regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't know of KLA killings of Albanian collaborationists, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We have heard rumors about this, but this was not a fact that was of crucial importance for our deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It was not a fact that was made apparent to you by any of your intelligence sources?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: As I told you, in the discussion or in the attempt to assess which side got it right and which got it wrong, the killing among the Albanians was not a factor which -- to which we attached the utmost priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you attach any priority to it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We saw that in this part of Europe and, unfortunately, a lot of violence took place which was alien to the rest of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is that another way of saying you did indeed know of killings of Albanian collaborationists or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We heard about it, but we didn't have corroborated intelligence on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You did hear about it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Asked and answered several times, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think at any stage that questioning got out of proportion and we now have the answers. Carry on, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll ask you about one matter in this memorandum. It talks on page 2, you'll see, General: "A new area of military engagement became gradually active since February as apparent the KLA from other regions moved to villages south-west of Kacanik near the southern border with the FRY with Macedonia." And it talks about an estimated 2.000 people fled villages in the Kacanik area, some trying to cross at the border to FRY of Macedonia. And, generally, what that paragraph refers to - at least that is what appears to me, General, and I'm suggesting this to you - that the KLA was attempting to provide an access route for a NATO ground invasion through that area, through that Kacanik-Kotlina area, and do you have knowledge of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that, and I can assure you what is also public knowledge, Mr. Sepenuk, that NATO never had any intention to attack with ground forces from Macedonia into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Was that also the KVM assessment, sir? Was that the assessment of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The KVM knew exactly that we did never had this intention; and by the way, NATO's political leadership at all levels stated again and again that we don't use ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have information to the contrary, sir. So let me refer you to 3D386. And while that's being put up, this is a statement by Christopher John Clark. And Christopher John Clark was the KVM operations officer for Kosovo. His responsibility was the management and coordination of the Kosovo field patrols. He would task the patrols on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if the usher would turn to page 8 of that report, I'd be grateful. And could you scroll up, please, go down to the last two lines, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You'll notice beginning at the last two lines, General, this is what Officer Stewart said -- Officer Clark said: "Also in late February/early March 1999, KLA forces infiltrated into the Kotlina area in southern Kosovo. The brigade had not previously been seen in Kosovo and was believed to have been infiltrated across the Macedonian border. After they came into Kosovo, we identified them and placed a team with them." And then he goes on to say at the bottom of the next paragraph: "The KVM assessment at the time was that the KLA was attempting to provide an access for NATO ground invasion through this area." So is it your contention that this gentleman who was on the ground got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: He's -- he's speculating about something for which he didn't have any justification at all, since there were no NATO plans to go with ground forces into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think this -- this statement of this KVM assessment is, in my view, speculation which is absolutely based on nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. And the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The real issue, I suppose, that we may have to look at is whether the Yugoslav authorities might have been justified in forming a similar view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know to which extent this assessment, Your Honour, was shared with the Yugoslav authorities. I suspect it was, since OSCE is a pretty transparent organisation. But the Yugoslav authorities knew from the highest leadership of -- of the NATO nations that we had no political intentions to go with ground forces into Yugoslavia, and they also knew that it was explicitly ruled out that ground forces would be used in a Kosovo contingency operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the sort of situation that NATO was facing, though, is it common to announce your intentions in that way and expect them to be believed by your potential opponents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- Your Honour, it's not common. And I can say in all sincerity here that I, as a military, I was absolutely unhappy with the statement, since you may remember that a famous German general once said that: "In a conflict the best plan is worthless as soon as the first contact with the enemy takes place." That was Mauker [phoen] and this is still true. So all your planning has to be based on the option that one is prepared to see a military operation through. And we, the NATO military, were deprived of that option when the ground forces were ruled out through political decision, but we had to accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The last document I want to show you, General, is P641. And, General, this is -- this was an annex to a statement by -- made by General Drewienkiewicz, General DZ, which is subject -- assessment of KLA attitudes as of March 15, 1999. That's about a week or so -- more than a week before the war started, and if you would turn to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher would put page 3 up, it's K0078050. Right. And if you would scroll down to the bottom, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it talks about -- first, it says, and I'll just read it to you. It's not up on the board, but I'll read it because it's brief. The report starts out: "Assessment of KLA attitudes as of March 15, 1999." And by the way, this is a report by David Wilson, who the evidence shows was the OSCE representative to one of the OSCE representatives, General, to the KLA, one of the KVM representatives to the KLA, sort of embedded with the KLA to a certain extent. And he says: "Their lines of command," referring to the KLA, "and control from the General Staff to the zone commanders and below seem to be generally effective." And then he goes on to say says -- that's what you have in front of you: "Recent events." And he talks about Kacanik in southern Kosovo and VJ activity in the border region of Kacanik. "The KLA fighters moved into the area. This inevitably led to clashes with the security forces, and eventually to a plan and thorough military operation to remove them from the area." And he goes on to say: "During the build-up to this operation, the KLA brigade commander in the area refused to let the UNHCR," United Nations high commissioner for refugees, "evacuate the displaced persons, the IDPs from the area. This has been seen as a cynical attempt to use Albanian civilians as a human shield." And he goes on to cite various other events concerning a KLA detaining a VJ soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if you go to the next page, please, the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Detain VJ soldier, a Dulje heights ambush, a Lebane shooting, and then he also talked about kidnap Albanian police employee. He says: "The KLA General Staff admitted that the Albanian police employee was arrested by the KLA security service for being a spy and that he's being held at their information centre. This is the first time that the KLA have admitted to having a region-wide police unit that conducts this type of operation. Again, the General Staff were not willing to acknowledge that this return to terrorist kidnappings was not to their benefit." Now, did this information come to you if not in this form in some other form, General? Did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Not in this detail I should say, but it fits more or less to what I had also stated in the Milosevic trial, that the KLA tried to fill the vacuum and created more or less semi-territorial authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, we're now about a week away from the war, and given that last report and considering we've had testimony here by Colonel Zyrapi, and the substance of that was by the time the war started the KLA had the advantage of moving from a form of guerilla army to a much more organised stronger army with some 17.000 to 18.000 men, combined with, if necessary, a hit-and-run guerilla advantage and with the support of thousands of Kosovar Albanian citizens. Isn't that a fair assessment, General?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- if I look at the events which then unfolded, I wouldn't see it as a fair assessment. I would see it as an expression of hope perhaps on the side of the KLA, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you disagree with --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't even know the man?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I did not know the man, but this fits with -- your statement fits into the theory that some of the KLA regarded NATO as their air-force. We never saw ourselves as the KLA air-force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In fact, General, what I'm suggested to you what happened here is that the Holbrooke agreement and then the Naumann-Clark agreement -- the Naumann-Clark-Milosevic agreement allowed the KLA, which had been under severe pressure in the fall of 1998, to retrieve its position as Yugoslav forces withdrew in fulfilment of the agreement. Instead of maintaining a is it fair to say, as required by UN Security Council Resolution 1199, the KLA went on the offensive. Yugoslav forces responded; and for that, General, Yugoslavia was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He didn't have one there. I object. I move to strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the closing argument, is it? I don't think you've required to answer that, Mr. Naumann, unless you particularly feel the need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in my view this is an assessment of -- on the side of Mr. Sepenuk, which obviously was not shared by the political leaders of 16 NATO nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General Naumann, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic. I take it you don't know General Pavkovic, and you've never met him. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No. I don't think that I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about some things you said in your direct examination and in your just-recently-completed cross-examination. You talked about NATO not having any kind of a plan for a ground attack. Are you familiar with a couple of operations called arrow 1 and arrow 2?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Today you told us that in conversations with Milosevic, you heard him use the words "final solution." Prior to today, you had had at least two opportunities to read through statements, at least one opportunity to read through your testimony in Milosevic and to make corrections. And you made no corrections regarding that. It seems to me those are words that anyone who has studied 20th century history at all would immediately react to as being words that came from the Third Reich and what happened there. And that, I guess you'll agree, would be especially true of someone like General Clark?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It finally was, I think.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, I do not know to which extent General Clark was familiar with European history, as we Europeans are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the word "final solution" is well-known to the world over, that phrase, isn't it? Isn't it something General Clark would have snapped to immediately?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: For me, as I said today, to me it rings automatically a bell of alert, but I do not know whether this is true for General Clark or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it was true for everybody in this room when you said it today. You got a kind of startled response from everybody today because we all reacted to it, and I think General Clark would have, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, that matter so far as the witness is able to deal with it has been answered. The general point is one on which you can make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I find is curious, General, is that General Clark spoke about this incident in some detail quoting Milutinovic in his books, and those words "final solution" don't appear there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure he quoted Milutinovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant Milosevic. I meant Milosevic. That was a mistake. We all made mistakes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read General Clark's book. I know he did not mention the word "final solution," but being obliged as I -- as this proceeding today started, I can only state my recollection is "final solution." And I regret that I overlooked it, obviously, when I read this statement earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another thing that you talked about briefly today at page 32, line 12, you talked about the mistake that had been made by referring to the KLA as a group of terrorists and how that tended to handicap NATO's ability to deal with this situation. And I take it it's your position that it wasn't that they weren't a group of terrorists. But that because of NATO's position, once you had called them a group of terrorists then you were handcuffed. And because of the policy of not negotiating with terrorists, you then couldn't talk to them?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's correct, we couldn't talk to them. This doesn't rule that I had agreed with the assessment in -- in April 1998. And as I have also said in this court, I never regarded the KLA as an congregation of angels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally, with regard to today's testimony, again, back on this subject of NATO not using ground forces. You said that that unfortunately was a decision that was made by -- as a result of NATO members, and I take it that that decision had to do with an unwillingness to risk the lives of NATO ground forces in this situation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is -- that's your assessment. The nations never shared with us the reason why they took this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you about several matters relating to the NATO approach to the Kosovo issue. I think you would agree with me first of all that a sovereign state has an absolute right to maintain law and order within its boundaries?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Fully agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that a group of terrorists or terrorist insurgents trying to take over and make independent a portion of a state are in violation of the law and legitimate target of efforts to restore law and order?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: This, I think, is an assessment which presumably cannot be shared in all cases. It depends very much on the attitude of a state to -- in which way he treats his citizens. If a state uses repression and suppression of citizens, then it might lead to reactions on the side of the suppressed citizens, which the state who acts in such a way, in such an illegal way, may see as terrorist activities. But that, I think, is a highly political debate which may differ from country to country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Assuming that I'm correct that there is a legitimate [sic] insurgency, terrorist insurgency, and that a state can maintain law and order by trying to end that insurgency, it really is up to that sovereign state what forces and units it wants to use to accomplish the restoration of law and order, whether military or police or a combination of the two. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: There again, Mr. Ackerman, we enter a debate which I think -- in which you use an interpretation of national sovereignty which obviously is no longer shared by the United Nations, if I -- if I see correctly what they more recently called the responsibility to protect as a content of modern interpretation of sovereignty. But as I do not belong to the League of International Lawyers who have to judge on the modern interpretation of sovereignty or not, I think we should leave it with that. You referred to an interpretation of sovereignty which allows any head of state and any government to do to its citizens whatever the head of state wishes to do. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that -- you've misunderstood me then because that is not what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: At least, I would like to say that is not my understanding of national sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nor is it mine, and I'm sorry if I misled you in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, the question attributed to you started with the reference to a legitimate insurgency, terrorist insurgency. I take it you did not mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm trying to establish with you, General, is that if there is terrorism going on in a country or a terrorist insurgency, as you've sometimes referred to it, it is up to that country, the leaders in that country to determine what combination of forces, police and military, to use to put down that insurgency? I'm not suggesting that they can just start wiping out people right and left and civilians and everything else. But what forces they use is up to them.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: As long as they act in concurrence with established norms of international law and as long as they respond in a proportionate way, I would tend to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's appropriate in the case of what you might call an insurgency-type terrorism to use military forces to accomplish that goal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That depends on an -- on the individual state. This is a decision which each state has to take individually, and this also depends heavily on the type of forces such a state has available. In many cases police forces might be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I just suggested to you were pretty much your exact words in a speech you gave in Israel on September 12, 2005, regarding the use of military forces to combat terrorism, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I do not know what speech you refer to, and I do not know whether you really put it out of context. I do not belong to those people who believe that military forces are the proper instrument to combat terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a speech you gave in Herzelia in Israel 2005. Now, you must remember giving that speech, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said in that speech: "The military must be ready to support the police in combatting terrorism when called upon to do so."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Yeah. And I would not have the slightest problem with that statement since to support police forces in combatting terrorism is something quite normal. If you imagine for a moment - and I referred to the situation of my own country - that a terrorist attack might be executed in these days as we have seen by using aircraft, the German police forces are not equipped to deal with an attacking aircraft. In such case in accordance with our law, the state would be entitled to ask the military to support the police in the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't say anything like that in that speech in Israel. That's just coming out of your mouth today.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There you were talking about -- the title of your speech was: The Proper Use Of The Military To Combat Terrorism. And that's what you talked about, the use of military to combat terrorism. You didn't talk about aircraft attacks.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Would you kindly also mention that I said - and I think you just quoted that - in support of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, I did just quote that. I think that was fair to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Then we are -- we might be closer to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about your view of what are and are not legitimate military targets. I take it you'll agree in a situation where terrorist activity is going on, and especially the insurgent-type terrorist activity that you talked about in Israel, that if fire is being directed at your forces from a building, that that building then becomes a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Mr. Ackerman. If the police forces are sufficient to cope with that type of threat, then there is no need to include military into the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let me take the word "military" out. It just becomes a legitimate target and it does, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Then it becomes a legitimate target, that is agreed; then we are in the question of what is proportionate to such a threat and what is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're going to get into that. Trust me. We're going to go there. And you agreed also that that would be true, that a building would become a target if it's being used as a place from which to direct fire on your troops, even if it was a mosque or a church?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Of course, I have to agree, otherwise, I've -- I would deny all the principles which we have used in self-defence for -- throughout my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What if that building, rather than being used to direct fire on your forces, just had someone in it with a hand-held radio that was providing information about the location of your forces and directing fire from another place, does it become a target then, a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: From a legal point, presumably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What if it is a building that has no military personnel in it at all, but civilians who are passing military information along to your opponent forces?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: It might be very difficult to establish the evidence for that in such a way that you can justify the use of lethal force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It might be. It might be. And we'll probably talk about that a little bit later, too. Now, I take it you would agree that we go back to that first example, a building from which fire is being directed at your forces, that it would be appropriate to attack that building with conventional infantry forces; just send the forces down to the building to take out the shooter. That would be a way to do it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's one way, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that way would certainly risk the lives of those forces that are sent across toward that building to the extent that they become targets for the shooters, right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Could happen, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another way to attack to at that building and the person shooting from that building would be artillery, direct artillery at that building, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think it would be -- in such a case of not very reliable information, it would be a rather disproportionate way to react to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the reliable information is that you're getting shot at by people in that building. Now, if you can't direct artillery at that building, then how can NATO bomb from 15.000 feet on the theory that they're saving the lives of their pilots by doing that? How is that legitimate and this one not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: The question of the legitimacy of NATO's action in Kosovo was subject of various international inquiries; and as far as I recall, the legitimacy of NATO's action was not called into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and that's the point of my question. It's okay for NATO to bomb from 15.000 feet to protect the lives of their pilots. Why isn't it okay to artillery from a mile away to protect the lives of your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: We did not bomb from 15.000 feet to protect the lives of our pilots. We used military aircraft against military targets in order to enforce respect for international law and to reach an end of hostilities and to reach the return of some close to 1.000.000 people who had been expelled. That's, I think, a slight difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, why on earth then did NATO explain to persons who were interested in this that the reason they bombed from 15.000 feet was to keep their pilots from being hit by anti-aircraft fire and missiles? Why would they have explained that if that wasn't the reason?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I don't know whom you are quoting. In our deliberations in the military side of NATO, this aspect that you've just mentioned was not a decisive element.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm probably not going to find it as I stand here right now. And if I don't finish with you today, I'll certainly be able to share it with you in the morning. What if you had the capability -- there are several buildings from which people are directing fire at your troops. What if you had the capability to call in an air-strike? That would be okay, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: You are talking about a ground operation in which you call for air support?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, this case doesn't play any role in the Kosovo campaign, of which -- about which we are talking, since NATO did not commit ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about technically.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If you are talking about the hypothetical case --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: -- that ground forces are fighting other ground forces, then it is legitimate to call in air support. That's what we all do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is a legitimate operation in a military operation, is it not, to try to conduct that operation in a way that protects the lives of your own soldiers and forces?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: You have -- in my understanding, and I think that was the understanding of all NATO nations at the time, of course you do what you can do to protect your own forces. But we also always had in mind to reduce the damage to the people of the nation, which came under military operations, will be protected to the extent possible as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in protecting the people to the extent possible as well, would probably have suggested low-level -- a low-level air campaign instead of dropping cluster bombs from 15.000 feet?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: You probably have never flown in a low-level aircraft, and your statement would be different in you had did it. It is presumably much easier to direct precision fire if you fly from above 10.000 feet than if you are running in a low-level-flying aircraft in which you may have terrible difficulties to properly identify the target. But you should try to fly one day at 15 metres above the ground and then your statement will be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I was suggesting 15 metres, but I think it would be nice if the pilot could verify a target before he destroys it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is his obligation also when he flies at 15.000 feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. But he can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, he has sufficient other means. He doesn't need his eyes. He has a lot of indications in the cockpit which may allow him to really hit a target quite accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. We'll get to that pretty soon, too. We're coming there. Would you agree with this statement: "A legitimate target is any facility that makes an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture, or neutralisation in the circumstances ruling at the time offers a definite military advantage?"

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: In principle, I would agree. I add, again, the question of proportionality has to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think that you'd also agree that the problem with the principle of proportionality is to determine what it means and how it's to be applied?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's exactly why I said it has to be considered, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For instance, if you decided to attack a refugee camp because people there are knitting socks for the army, that would be clearly disproportionate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I cannot imagine that anyone attacks a refugee camp deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the other hand, if you're attacking an ammo dump and there happens to be a farmer ploughing a field next door and gets killed in that process, that is a legitimate target and he was collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, to attack an ammunition dump, I think, is absolutely legitimate in an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course, it is.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That collateral damages occur is something that nobody regrets more than those people responsible for military operations, but you unfortunately cannot rule it out entirely. But I would invite you to look into the statistics of the Kosovo air campaign to see that the collateral damage is really pretty low. And a lot of independent observers agreed -- yeah, testified that NATO took utmost care in avoiding collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's another thing we're going to get into as we go along, but you wanted to talk about statistics. And I'm going to find those for you. Unfortunately, my assistant here lost my page. Tell me if you agree with these statistics. During the bombing campaign, NATO aircraft flew 38.400 sorties, 10.484 strike sorties. During those sorties, 23.614 air munitions were released and 500 civilians were killed, approximately. Would you agree with those statistics?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I know them. And the only thing which I could add is 500 civilians are 500 too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, nobody's going to disagree with that, of course. Now, when we were talking about these two extreme examples that I just talked to you about, the knitting of socks for the army and the attack on an ammunition dump, what I was trying to do is give you extreme examples where one is clearly not legitimate or the other clearly is. And, unfortunately, most of the situations that we run across are somewhere in between those two, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is a -- I think it's an assessment which I wouldn't share.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. Most of them are in between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I guess we'll get to that in a little while also. Would you agree with this: It's much easier to formulate a principle of proportionality in general terms than it is to apply it to a particular set of circumstances because the comparison is often unlike quantities and values. One cannot easily assess the value of human lives as opposed to capturing a particular military objective. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure whether I would agree with this generality. I agree that it is extremely difficult to apply the principle for proportionality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. A military barracks housing soldiers of the enemy, even though there are numerous non-combatants there providing logistical assistance, cooking facilities, clothing repair, that sort of thing, it doesn't become a nontarget just because the noncombatants are present, does it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: A military facility, a military barrack is I think a target which can be attacked. Again, the principle of avoiding unnecessary collateral damage has to be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And we did this, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. And if -- and if, as we see in -- in the current asymmetrical situations that exist in the world today, terrorists will sometimes set up what amounts to barracks in a civilian area. In Kosovo, it was seen in the family compounds in the various villages. And they'll be sleeping there at night; they'll be taking meals there. It's a place that for all practical purposes is a barracks. That's also a legitimate target, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: I think we -- I do not recall any target of the way -- of the kind you described that we used as a target in the NATO targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A decision to attack such a facility like the one I just talked about has to be based on intelligence, surveillance, something to give you some sense of what the conditions are that prevail there. And I think you'll agree that's what's required of a commander in these situations is that he do his best to obtain reliable information before he acts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That's -- you're stating your personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And an important question is to what extent is that military commander obligated to expose his own forces to danger in order to limit civilian casualties and correct civilian objects. And that's an important question that always has to be asked by the commander, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let's take this hypothetical situation: You have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you've already acknowledged that this whole trial, indeed Tribunal, is beset by problems of time. The review of hypothetical situations and matters which may be matters of legal interpretation don't, at first sight, appear to be the best way of making use of the presence of this witness when there are so many actual factual situations that might be explored of which he has either direct knowledge or has gathered knowledge in the course of his work. Could we not get to the -- more directly to the circumstances of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will get there. I do want to -- to suggest to you that, in my view, a significant part of this witness's evidence is his evidence that in his view the actions of Serb forces were disproportionate to the situation, and that is certainly a legal issue, an issue of law. What's disproportionate and what is not disproportionate is really for Your Honours to determine. And so I think I'm entitled to explore with him this issue of disproportionality, and what that is and what that means to him and how he views it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But can I give you an example which isn't one that we are considering at this stage, at least in the case. In Racak, for example, you might give the general -- the facts from the Serb side, and then let's hear him tell us what he thinks about it. Now, why is it you dance around the subject in hypothetical questions and don't get to the actual facts that may be relevant to your quest for opinions from him? He's not here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And his opinions are only really of significance in relation to matters of which he has some personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- and if the Chamber is prepared to ignore his evidence that some of these attacks in his view were disproportionate because he's not here as an expert, then I'm -- I don't have near as much to talk to him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's because he's got facts in his head on the basis of which he has expressed that view. And if you want to challenge him on that, then I would see not only force in you doing it but the provision of assistance to us, because we lack that information at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, my next question, actually, Your Honour I think goes where you're suggesting I should go, and that is into things we have heard in this case. It's hypothetical, but it does refer to -- and you'll recognise it immediately, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Assume that you're a commander who has information that there is a village that is engaged in heavy support for your enemy and that enemy forces are quartered there. You decide to attack that village, but you understand there are civilians there. And out of concern for those civilians, you begin by firing artillery over the top of that village, in the hopes that that will frighten that population, that civilian population into abandoning the village and, thereby, having their lives saved. Would that make sense to you to do that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: No, no. But it wouldn't make sense to me, and I wouldn't do that if I were a military commander. Perhaps -- Your Honour, and you permit me that -- first of all, make two general remarks before I answer your question, Mr. Ackerman, very precisely. The first one is when I state disproportionate use of force, then it was -- I referred to a statement, to an assessment to which the NATO council came by looking at the situation. So it is an agreement -- it was an assessment which already 16 NATO nations arrived at, not in -- not only me as a person. Secondly, to clarify the role of the chairman of the military committee in selecting targets, it was not my task to select individual targets nor was it the task of General Clark. What I did was to issue guidance to General Clark that this and this and this category of targets is approved by the NATO council, and then to monitor whether he stayed within the guidance. But I never -- I never looked of -- I never looked into individual targets unless we came to a situation where the risk of collateral damage was too big. To give you an example, since you obviously like precise examples, General Clark approached me on one -- in one situation with the request to bomb the headquarters of the police in central down-town Belgrade. And he had I think ample justification for doing that. I asked him -- then it was the only time that I was involved in an individual targeting. I asked him, Please tell me, how does this target look like in its surrounding? I do not want to see that any collateral damage is done, and please tell me how many munitions you will use to achieve your tactical purpose. He told -- he gave me that information, and I told him, Based on that, I will not recommend to the secretary-general of NATO to give you the authority to do this, since the risk of collateral damage being done to the hospital in Belgrade is by far too big. So go back and do your targeting again and show me that you can do it in a way which will reduce the risk. That was the only time, Mr. Ackerman, that I looked into an individual target. Otherwise, my task was to make sure that we stayed within the political agreed limits and that we did not do anything which was beyond the guidance we had given. Now coming to your wonderful --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me say that is very commendable and we all applaud you for that decision as the right decision.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: Well, the building was bombed anyway, but there was no collateral damage. That is the thing for which I think I am grateful that it was done in that way. But now to answer your question. If the situation were as such you described it, I would regard the use of artillery in such a situation as the first response of a military officer as being disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not directed at any target.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: If you can take out an objective, I would in such a situation use first infantry forces and attack the village or this group of buildings with infantry forces. The targets which you describe do not require to use tanks or artillery, and that is perhaps our different understanding of what might be proportionate and what not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how do you protect the civilians in that situation, especially if you know that the insurgents wear civilian clothes, they drop their arms when they see someone coming near? How do you distinguish --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is something which is -- I admit, it's extremely difficult. And I can also tell you, I have to do this myself when I was a student at the Royal College of Defence Studies in London. They took us to their training camp where they trained for the Northern Ireland insurgency, and they exposed me exactly to the situation you just described. And every one of us doing individual patrolling with a live-fire rifle, every one of us who hit a civilian target passed the course. So -- did not pass the course. So I think we -- I tell you this detail to indicate to you that we tried to educate our soldiers really to avoid any individual -- any collateral damage and that we really tried to punish those who hit the wrong targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the earlier matter of the bombing of the police headquarters, who had the authority to make the decision to carry out the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, Your Honour, since it would have been one of the first attacks on down-town Belgrade, the secretary-general of NATO had to agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that must have been agreed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the political level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but agreed contrary to your advice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on my advice, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this -- this last issue we've been talking about, this village that you would attack with infantry forces basically. As a commander, what do you think is the -- the maximum number of your soldiers you would have be killed before you decide to change your tactic? How many are you prepared to sacrifice to that situation before you use artillery?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That is, again, Mr. Ackerman, is a decision which you can never take in a hypothetical scenario. You have to see what is happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and that's exactly my point, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: You have -- I think your desire is always to protect as much human life as possible, and I say deliberately on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, in that situation if you could have this giant loud-speaker and say, Attention, civilians, leave town. We're going to start firing at the troops that are in your town. That might be a way to help protect the civilians there.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: And things like this were done in real war and things like this are done again and again in exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you did that, the civilians might come to this court and say, They told me if I didn't leave my village they would can I have me?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: You mean the people who were sitting in the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whose lives you were trying to save. That could happen, too?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: That could happen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If a military organisation of some kind decides to take over a civilian building, a civilian compound, these compounds that existed in Kosovo or do exist in Kosovo, is it not the obligation of that military force then to remove the civilians from that compound to protect them from just the thing we were talking about and not to use them as human shields, for instance?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN
utterances.text: To use civilians as human shields is in my view a crime, and under no circumstance -- can in no circumstances be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to break now, Your Honour? I see it's 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it is an appropriate time to break. I'm just considering that last question. You're not going to follow it with a question about the appropriate conduct of the opposing military force when that doesn't happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably not, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We've now run out of time for today, I'm afraid, Mr. Naumann. So we will adjourn until tomorrow, and we'll be sitting at 9.00 tomorrow. Meanwhile, as I'm sure you know very well, it's vital that you have no discussion with anyone at all overnight about the evidence, either that you've given or that you may yet give in this case and deal -- talk about other matters entirely. Come back here refreshed, due to recommence at 9.00 tomorrow. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect we're well out with the guide-lines that have been given in relation to cross-examination, but I hope nevertheless that counsel are all alert to the need to complete cross-examination within the guide-lines as far as possible or as close as you can to these guide-lines. We'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of December, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.03 p.m.,
